title: The illness
hook: he falls ill and is nursed in Aisha's room

segments.voice: Yesterday, this day I have perfected: the verse at Arafah that said the religion was whole. Your line was completed. What did you finish all the way? Day two hundred eighty-seven, the end of the week.

Almost everyone has sat beside a hospital bed or a sickbed at home. You know the room: the curtains half drawn, the glass of water on the side table, people talking in lowered voices in the hall. A few months after the farewell pilgrimage, back in Medina, the Prophet ﷺ began to suffer from a severe headache and fever. It didn't pass. He kept going to the mosque as long as he could, and he kept to his custom of spending each night with one of his wives in turn. But he grew weaker, and he kept asking, the reports say: where am I tomorrow? Today, the room he chose.
screen: `A SICKBED IN MEDINA.` → `HEADACHE AND FEVER.` → `WHERE AM I TOMORROW?`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari tells it through Aisha. When the illness grew heavy, he asked his wives for permission to be nursed in her room, and they all agreed. Notice that: even then, even sick, he asked. He walked there leaning on two men, his feet dragging a line in the dirt. That small room, next to the mosque, is where the last days of his life happened. The companions came in and out. His daughter Fatimah came. Aisha nursed him. And what was he doing with visitors all his life? Visiting the sick himself. The hadith collections are full of it: he visited the sick of Medina, rich and poor, and once, the reports say, he visited a Jewish boy who had served him and was dying. He listed visiting the sick among the rights one Muslim has over another. And there's a hadith qudsi, words he reported from God, preserved in Sahih Muslim, that turns this into something stunning. On the Day of Judgment, God will say: son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit Me. And the person says: how could I visit You, when You are the Lord of the worlds? And God says: my servant was sick and you did not visit him. Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him. That's our word today: the Arabic 'iyadah, visiting the sick. And it closes a week of hard lessons: numbers didn't help, the truth saved them, they came from everywhere, all in white, no one above another, completed. Now, the sickroom.
screen: `EVEN SICK, HE ASKED PERMISSION.` · `THE ROOM BESIDE THE MOSQUE.` · `HE HAD ALWAYS VISITED THE SICK.` · `YOU WOULD HAVE FOUND ME WITH HIM.` · then, large: `VISIT THE SICK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: visit or call someone sick. Sit for a moment, and breathe. Who's unwell in your life right now? Someone in the hospital, someone with an illness that's gone on so long people have stopped asking, someone recovering at home, someone struggling in their mind. Picture them, and picture the room they're in. Decide how you'll reach them after the bell: a visit, a call, a message, a meal left at the door. If you pray, you can pray for their healing now. The bell holds the time.
The illness. The Prophet's last sickness, nursed in Aisha's room, and a reminder of how he always visited the sick. Today's word.
Your line: visit the sick. Today, reach one person who's unwell. Five minutes of your voice may be the best part of their day. Day two hundred eighty-seven.

screen: `DAY 287 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ABU BAKR LEADS THE PRAYER.`

howItsDone: Muslims count visiting the sick, 'iyadah, as a right owed between Muslims and a deed of great reward; many make a point of visiting relatives, neighbors and strangers in the hospital and praying for their healing.

fork.setup: you're gravely ill, and you want to be nursed in one room instead of moving between your wives' houses. what do you do?
fork.reveal: he asked, and they all agreed. even very sick, he asked permission.

original.note: Arabic: visiting the sick. counted in the hadith among the rights Muslims owe one another.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Prophet got sick at the end.
what it means: his last days in a sickroom, asking permission, after a life of visiting the sick.
what a scholar hears: Aisha's account in al-Bukhari, and the hadith qudsi in Sahih Muslim 2569 where God identifies with the sick: you would have found Me with him.
